content: In healthy individuals, urine within the bladder is sterile, meaning it contains no bacteria or other infectious organisms. The urethra, which carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body, typically harbors no bacteria or only a minimal amount insufficient to cause infection. However, any part of the urinary tract can become infected. The presence of typical urinary pathogens is considered clinically significant when obtained via suprapubic aspiration. An infection occurring anywhere along the urinary tract is termed a urinary tract infection (UTI), which is the second most common infection in children. UTIs are caused by bacteria entering the urethral opening and ascending to the bladder, and in some cases, the kidneys. In severe cases, bacteria may enter the bloodstream from the kidneys, leading to sepsis or infections in other organs. During infancy, boys are more prone to developing UTIs, but after infancy, girls are at a significantly higher risk. Children with UTIs often have structural abnormalities in their urinary system, predisposing them to infection. These abnormalities include vesicoureteral reflux (VUR), a condition where urine flows backward from the bladder to the kidneys, and other conditions that obstruct urine flow. Delayed diagnosis and treatment of UTIs in children, particularly infants, can increase the risk of renal scarring, which may progress over time. The primary goals of UTI management in children are to alleviate symptoms, prevent renal damage, and reduce the risk of recurrence. Identifying and addressing structural or functional factors, as well as treating voiding dysfunction and constipation, are critical for successful management. Since the 1970s, clinicians evaluating febrile infants without an identifiable source of infection have focused on occult bacteremia. However, with the advent of effective conjugate vaccines against Haemophilus influenzae type b and Streptococcus pneumoniae, which have significantly reduced bacteremia and meningitis, the urinary tract has been increasingly recognized as a common site of occult and serious bacterial infections. Diagnosing UTIs in infants can be challenging due to nonspecific clinical presentations and the need for invasive methods, such as urethral catheterization or suprapubic aspiration, to obtain reliable urine specimens. Delays in initiating appropriate treatment for pyelonephritis have been shown to increase the risk of renal damage. UTIs can be classified based on the site of infection (bladder, kidney, or urethra), severity (complicated versus uncomplicated), and recurrence (first episode or recurrent). In healthy children, the urinary tract is typically sterile, while the urethra is colonized with bacteria. UTIs occur when pathogens enter the urinary tract and adhere to its lining. Normal voiding usually clears pathogens from the bladder, but conditions such as urinary malformations, urine stasis, or impaired urine flow increase the risk of infection by providing a reservoir for bacteria and allowing time for bacterial adherence to the uroepithelial mucosa. Congenital obstructive uropathy and detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia, which impair bladder emptying, are also associated with UTIs. Another mechanism involves the introduction of pathogens via foreign bodies or instruments, such as catheters. UTIs are the third most common nosocomial infection in intensive care units, following bloodstream infections and pneumonia. Nosocomial UTIs are frequently associated with urethral catheterization, and Escherichia coli accounts for 80–90% of pediatric UTIs. Among febrile infants, unwell children, and older children with urinary symptoms, 6–8% will have a UTI. Symptoms of pyelonephritis include fever, chills, rigor, flank pain, and costovertebral angle tenderness. Lower urinary tract symptoms include suprapubic pain, dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, cloudy or malodorous urine, and suprapubic tenderness. When a UTI is suspected, urinalysis and urine culture should be performed. While awaiting culture results, prompt antibiotic therapy is recommended for symptomatic UTIs based on clinical findings and positive urinalysis to improve outcomes. The prevalence of UTIs varies with age, peaking in young infants, toddlers, and older adolescents. UTIs are more common in females and uncircumcised male infants. During toilet training, volitional holding and bladder stasis can promote UTIs. Over 30% of children with a UTI will experience recurrence, with common risk factors including VUR and bladder-bowel dysfunction. Older non-continent children, such as those with developmental delays, are also at higher risk for recurrent UTIs. The most common pathogens causing UTIs in children are enteric bacteria, particularly Escherichia coli, which accounts for over 80% of cases. Other gram-negative organisms include Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterobacter, and occasionally Pseudomonas. Proteus mirabilis is a common pathogen in males and children with kidney stones. Gram-positive pathogens include group B Streptococcus and Enterococcus in neonates and infants, reflecting maternal colonization, and Staphylococcus saprophyticus in adolescent girls. Fungal infections, though rare, are more likely in immunocompromised children, those with diabetes, or those with long-term indwelling catheters. Candida is the most common fungal pathogen. Viral UTIs are more common in immunocompromised patients, with adenovirus and BK virus being notable causes of hemorrhagic cystitis. In children under 24 months, fever may be the only presenting symptom of a UTI. However, physical examination findings may suggest alternative diagnoses, such as otitis media, gastroenteritis, or upper respiratory tract infections. Occult bacteremia should also be considered, though it is less likely than a UTI in fully immunized children without another identifiable source of fever. In verbal children with urinary symptoms, differential diagnoses include urinary calculi, urethritis (including sexually transmitted infections), dysfunctional elimination, and diabetes mellitus. Neonates and infants are at higher risk for UTIs due to their immature immune systems. Breastfeeding appears to provide protection against UTIs, likely due to higher levels of IgA in breast milk. Approximately 8% of girls and 2% of boys experience at least one UTI by age 7. The incidence of UTIs is similar in boys and girls under 2 years of age but becomes more common in girls as they grow older, particularly in sexually active teenagers. Uncircumcised infant boys are at higher risk for UTIs. Structural abnormalities, neurologic deficiencies, or voiding dysfunction can contribute to persistent bacteriuria. In developed countries, UTIs are more common in white girls than in girls of other races, and the incidence is lower in African-American children. Risk factors for UTIs include being female, particularly during toilet training, due to the shorter urethra and proximity to the anus. Uncircumcised boys under one year of age also have a slightly higher risk. Other risk factors include structural abnormalities, vesicoureteral reflux, poor hygiene, infrequent urination, and constipation. Common complications of UTIs in children include kidney abscesses, reduced kidney function or failure, hydronephrosis, and sepsis. Prognosis is generally good with prompt treatment, but children with recurrent UTIs or VUR may require long-term management, including antibiotic prophylaxis or surgery in severe cases. Diagnosis of UTIs in children often begins with a urinalysis and urine culture. In infants and young children, urine samples are typically obtained via catheterization to avoid contamination. Imaging studies, such as ultrasound or voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG), may be recommended in certain cases to evaluate for structural abnormalities or VUR. Additional diagnostic tools include DMSA scans, CT, or MRI. Treatment of UTIs in children typically involves antibiotics, with secondor third-generation cephalosporins and amoxicillin-clavulanate being the drugs of choice for uncomplicated cases. Parenteral antibiotics are recommended for infants under two months or children who are toxic, hemodynamically unstable, or unable to tolerate oral medications. Continuous antibiotic prophylaxis may be considered for children with frequent febrile UTIs, though it is not routinely justified. Surgery is reserved for cases where medical management fails, such as recurrent infections or poor renal growth. Addressing related health issues may also help reduce the risk of UTIs.
